Learning Objectives
Identify a progressive collapsing foot deformity via an in-depth patient history and physical
examination.
Detect associated factors, stage the condition, and define a treatment rationale for a
progressive collapsing foot deformity.
Use imaging studies as an auxiliary measure to distinguish and stage different presentations of
a progressive collapsing foot deformity and construct a proper therapeutic plan.

Definition

Definition
In 2020, a group of experienced orthopaedic foot and ankle specialists proposed a
change in the nomenclature from the most common terminology, adult-acquired flatfoot
deformity, to progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD).1-3 The objective of the
proposed change in terminology was to better describe the progressive and collapsing
character of the deformity and to reveal that the condition is not restricted to adults,
may not be acquired, and that flattening of the longitudinal arch is just one aspect of this
complex three-dimensional and multifocal deformity.1 Recent data also support that the
posterior tibial tendon is only one of the medial soft-tissue structures involved in the
pathology and typically is less affected than ligamentous components, such as the spring
and talocalcaneal interosseus ligaments, with deficiency of the posterior tibial tendon
likely representing a consequence rather than a cause of the deformity.1,2,4,5 Although
this terminology has gained traction in the foot and ankle community, the universal
adoption across the broader field of orthopaedics has been more gradual. Regardless,
examination of the accepted pathophysiology of complex conditions is important, and
this paradigm shift should be considered.6
Clinical Diagnosis
Patient History
Medial foot and ankle pain
Swelling at the medial aspect of the foot and ankle
Pain and swelling at the lateral aspect of the foot (lateral impingement)
Change in the foot shape (flatfoot, collapse of the longitudinal arch)
Altered gait and foot strike

Patient History

In the classic clinical presentation, patients commonly report pain at the medial aspect
of the foot and ankle along the trajectory of the posterior tibial tendon and the plantar-
medial soft-tissue structures. The structures are progressively and chronically
overloaded under tension by the deformity, with collapse of the longitudinal arch, valgus
and external rotation of the hindfoot, abduction of the midfoot/forefoot, and relative
supination of the forefoot.7-10
Reactive synovitis of the overloaded medial tendons and joints may produce an
inflammatory response, resulting in effusion and edema in this region7,8 (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Clinical photograph of a foot shows medial swelling around the medial soft-
tissue structures, which is a common complaint in patients with progressive collapsing
foot deformity. (Courtesy of Cesar de Cesar Netto, MD, PhD, Iowa City, IA.)
As the deformity progresses, external rotation and valgus of the hindfoot result in
impingement of the lateral aspect of the talus into the floor of the sinus tarsi (sinus tarsi
impingement) and impingement of the lateral aspect of the calcaneus and/or talus into
the distal fibula (subfibular impingement). Pain and swelling develop at the lateral aspect
of the foot and ankle, usually in the subfibular and sinus tarsi areas.4,9-14

Patients often report that their foot is collapsing. Individuals with a previous deformity
(from childhood or adolescence) may state that the deformity has worsened8 (Figure 2).
Similar to changes in foot shape and alignment, patients also may perceive changes in
gait, specifically less stability and weakness at push-off and/or pain with ambulation.15,16
Figure 2 Clinical photograph of bilateral legs of a patient with progressive collapsing foot
deformity shows a change in foot and ankle alignment. Note the increased asymmetric
hindfoot valgus alignment on the left side. (Courtesy of Cesar de Cesar Netto, MD, PhD,
Iowa City, IA.)
Physical Examination
Inspection of alignment: heel valgus, flatfoot, and forefoot abduction
Gait: medial sagging, second rocker diminishing, difficulty in the push-off phase
Too-many-toes sign
Single-leg heel rise test
Jack test

Forefoot supination
Hindfoot inversion strength (posterior tibial muscle strength)
Medial column instability

Physical Examination
With the patient standing, valgus of the heel is commonly observed from behind.
Flattening of the longitudinal arch of the foot presents in different degrees of severity by
observing the patient’s foot from the medial side. Forefoot abduction, a perception that
the distal segment of the foot deviates laterally, is observed from the front or from
behind (too-many-toes sign)17,18 (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Clinical photographs of the foot and ankle of a patient with progressive
collapsing food deformity show static posterior inspection, revealing increased hindfoot
valgus (A), longitudinal arch collapse (B), and forefoot abduction (C). (Courtesy of Cesar
de Cesar Netto, MD, PhD, Iowa City, IA.)
During the stance phase of gait, an exaggerated (and asymmetric if unilateral) sagging in
the medial aspect of the foot may be present. As the deformity progresses, the second
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:54 PM

rocker decreases in length because of pain. Push-off is hindered by the absence of
optimal locking of the midtarsal joints.7,10,16,17
In a patient standing with the feet parallel and pointing forward, normally only the fifth
and half of the fourth toes can be observed from behind. A too-many-toes sign is
present if the third (or the second) toe can be observed. This is because of hindfoot
valgus/external rotation, particularly the midfoot/forefoot abduction component of the
PCFD8 (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Clinical photograph of the foot of a patient with progressive collapsing foot
deformity shows the too-many-toes sign and pronounced midfoot/forefoot abduction.
The entire second toe and part of the first toe are visible. (Courtesy of Cesar de Cesar
Netto, MD, PhD, Iowa City, IA.)
Joint and deformity flexibility, posterior tibial tendon and triceps surae strength, and the
integrity of the windlass mechanism are assessed via the single-leg heel rise test. In this
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:54 PM

test, the patient is asked to stand on his or her tiptoes while lifting the contralateral foot
off the ground, using a wall for support. During a normal single-leg heel rise, the heel
moves into varus, the longitudinal arch increases, and the leg externally rotates. As PCFD
progresses, patients may be unable to perform the test secondary to weakness or, if the
valgus deformity is rigid, the hindfoot deformity may not correct to the expected varus,
potentially guiding management7,8,17,19 (Figure 5; Video 1).
Figure 5 Clinical photographs show the single-leg heel rise test. A, Photograph of
bilateral legs of a patient who has a flexible progressive collapsing foot deformity and
relatively preserved posterior tibial tendon muscle strength shows a normal left-heel rise
test. B, Photograph of bilateral legs of a patient with a rigid progressive collapsing foot
deformity shows an altered right-heel rise test. (Courtesy of Cesar de Cesar Netto, MD,
PhD, Iowa City, IA.)

Originally described for flexibility evaluation in children, the jack test also may be used in
adults. The jack test assesses subtalar flexibility and the integrity of the windlass
mechanism. With the patient standing, the hallux is passively dorsiflexed at the
metatarsophalangeal joint by the examiner. Testing of a normal foot will result in an
increase in the longitudinal arch height, varus of the heel, and external rotation of the
leg. In patients with PCFD and rigid deformities, these changes will not be observed and
may alter treatment planning19 (Video 2).

Video 2 de Cesar Netto C: Video. Jack Test. Iowa City, IA, 2021.
The Silfverskiöld test assesses tightness of the calf muscles and is commonly used to
distinguish an isolated gastrocnemius contracture from combined gastrocnemius and
soleus contractures. While keeping the heel in a neutral or varus position and locking the
midtarsal joints, passive ankle dorsiflexion is assessed with the knee in an extended
position followed by a flexed position. During the first step (knee extended), inability to
achieve 10° of ankle dorsiflexion confirms tightness of the gastrocnemius and soleus
muscles. During the second step (knee flexed), a relative increase in ankle dorsiflexion of
more than 10° is consistent with isolated tightness of the gastrocnemius muscle.
Absence of a relative increase in ankle dorsiflexion or a slight increase that is less than
10° also indicates the presence of combined tightness of the soleus and gastrocnemius
muscle1,7,20 (Video 3).

With the patient seated and the lower limbs hanging, hindfoot valgus is manually
reduced to neutral alignment while the forefoot is observed from the front. If relative
forefoot supination greater than 15° is present, then a forefoot supination deformity
(varus) is indicated, influencing staging and treatment planning1,7,8 (Figure 6).

observed. If relative forefoot supination greater than 15° is present, a forefoot

Active inversion strength should be tested against resistance. Pain and/or weakness
during active and resisted inversion may be signs of posterior tibial tendon involvement,
potentially influencing management.8,10,21
With the patient seated and both legs hanging freely, medial column mobility is assessed
by stabilizing the intermediate and lateral columns with one hand while producing
dorsal-plantar translation of the medial column with the other hand. More than 10 mm
of dislocation (or a complete dorsal overhaul) is an indication of medial column
hypermobility/instability, influencing management22,23 (Video 4).

Imaging Studies
Radiographs

Radiographs
Weight-bearing AP radiographs of the foot, AP or mortise radiographs of the ankle,
lateral radiographs of the foot, and a hindfoot alignment radiographs (Figure 7) are the
minimum conventional radiographic views recommended for the assessment of PCFD.9
Indirect signs of PCFD, such as superposition of the metatarsals, arch collapse, and talar
declination on a lateral view, may be observed on initial review.24 AP ankle radiographs
are important for identification of possible valgus deformity of the ankle, which is
indicated by talar tilt into the mortise (a finding that influences classification and
management; Figure 8).25


Lateral Foot Radiographs
The talus–first metatarsal angle is determined by the angle between the longitudinal
axes of the talus and the first metatarsal. Normal angles are between -4° and +4°, and
values greater than 4° are consistent with PCFD24,26 (Figure 9). 
Figure 9 Lateral weight-bearing radiograph of the foot and ankle of a patient with
progressive collapsing foot deformity demonstrates a talus–first metatarsal angle (Meary
angle) of 18°. (Courtesy of Cesar de Cesar Netto, MD, PhD, Iowa City, IA.)
The talocalcaneal angle is measured by the angle formed between the longitudinal axes
of the talus and the calcaneus.27 Angles from 25° to 45° are considered normal, whereas
values greater 45° are consistent with PCFD27 (Figure 10).

progressive collapsing foot deformity demonstrates a talocalcaneal angle (Kite angle) of
37°. (Courtesy of Cesar de Cesar Netto, MD, PhD, Iowa City, IA.)
Calcaneal pitch is an angle traced between the floor and a line tangent to the calcaneal
plantar surface, drawn from the most inferior point of the calcaneal tuberosity and along
the bottom edge of the calcaneal anterior process.26 Angles less than 17° are compatible
with PCFD26,28 (Figure 11).

Plantar gapping at the first tarsometatarsal or at the naviculocuneiform joints of more
than 2 mm are indirect signs of medial column instability. Dorsal displacement of the
first metatarsal and first tarsometatarsal arthritis also are considered potential findings
of first ray hypermobility/instability and should be considered in PCFD29 (Figure 12). 
Figure 12 Lateral weight-bearing radiograph of the foot and ankle of a patient with
progressive collapsing foot deformity demonstrates plantar gapping of the first
tarsometatarsal joint and mild dorsal displacement of the first metatarsal, both of which
are signs of medial column instability. (Courtesy of Cesar de Cesar Netto, MD, PhD, Iowa
City, IA.)


Weight-Bearing CT Scans
The advent of weight-bearing CT has enabled more complete and three-dimensional
assessment of PCFD and introduced new measurements and signs that may aid in early
diagnosis and disease management.31-35 In rigid PCFD, CT plays an important role in
identification of joint arthritis and possible tarsal coalitions. Important additional
findings optimized via weight-bearing CT assessment include the following:
Extra-articular contact between the talar lateral process and the floor of the sinus tarsi at
the calcaneus Gissane angle (which may be wrongfully recognized as posterior facet
subtalar joint arthritis on conventional radiographs) are signs of peritalar subluxation
and may be observed on coronal and sagittal CT scans4,8,9,12,14 (Figure 15).

Impingement of the distal fibula with the lateral aspect of the calcaneus and/or talus,
usually best observed on coronal weight-bearing CT scans, represents an indirect sign of
severe PCFD,9,14 with possible involvement of the ankle joint in the overall deformity or
severe involvement of the connecting ligaments between the talus and calcaneus4
(Figure 16).

Peritalar subluxation is a marker of hindfoot deformity in PCFD and is characterized by
progressive external rotation, abduction, and lateral displacement of the calcaneus
under the talus.1,4,36-40 Subtalar joint facets subluxate as disease and deformity
progress; this subluxation can be measured as a percentage of joint uncoverage on
coronal weight-bearing CT scans38,41,42 (Figures 15 and 16).
Increased angulation between the subtalar joint posterior talar facet with the floor line
(subtalar horizontal angle)31,43 or the talar dome joint line (superior talar/inferior talar
angle) in the coronal plane may represent a risk factor for PCFD40,44 (Figure 17).

Ultrasonography

Ultrasonography
Assessment of the degree of degeneration of all medial and plantar soft-tissue foot and
ankle structures has been shown to be important in the assessment of patients with
PCFD.5 Particularly, involvement of the posterior tibial tendon, deltoid, spring, and
talocalcaneal interosseus ligaments is part of the staging process for the pathology and

correlate with the amount of bony collapse and deformity severity.4,5 Ultrasonography is
an optional dynamic assessment of the same structures and a potentially useful and
accessible diagnostic imaging modality, particularly in the early presentation of PCFD,
supporting adequate differential diagnosis with other possible causes of medial foot and
ankle pain.7,45 As a dynamic imaging modality, ultrasonography has particular value in
assessing the magnitude of instability from ligament strain and disruption.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Posterior tibial tendon
Spring ligament
Deltoid complex

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Although ultrasonography may be considered, MRI remains the preferred imaging
modality for assessment of soft-tissue involvement in patients with PCFD. Degeneration
of the posterior tibial tendon, deltoid, spring, talocalcaneal interosseous, and cervical
ligaments should be assessed.1,4,5,46 Posterior tibial muscle fatty degeneration also can
be assessed via MRI of the leg and may influence surgical decision making.47
Intratendinous degeneration and inflammatory sheath distension are characteristic
findings if MRI is used to assess the diseased posterior tibial tendon. Retromalleolar and
insertional tendinopathy are the most common findings48 (Figure 18). Studies have
shown that posterior tibial tendon involvement seems to be less important and less
severe than the degeneration of other soft-tissue restrainers, such as the spring and
talocalcaneal interosseus ligaments.4,5

This structure originates from the sustentaculum tali and inserts at the medial and
plantar aspect of the navicular (and cuneiform). It serves as a sling and stabilizes the
talonavicular and subtalar joints. Degeneration of the spring ligament is very common in
patients with PCFD and correlates with sinus tarsi impingement.4,5 Adequate
assessment of this soft tissue can be performed via MRI49 (Figure 19). The condition of
the spring ligament may be evaluated on axial and coronal MRIs.

Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis
Several conditions may be associated with PCFD and present as initial indirect signs of
the deformity. Careful clinical and subsidiary evaluation is necessary to determine if each
of the following conditions are isolated, combined, or nonrelated diseases.8
The differential diagnosis for PCFD includes tarsal tunnel syndrome, plantar fascia
degeneration, Achilles tendinopathy, ankle impingement, calcaneal stress fracture,
medial malleolus stress fracture, medial talus osteochondral lesion, flexor hallucis

and accessory navicular.
Staging

Staging
The concept of categorizing disease progression into different stages was the basis of
prior classification systems, first described and introduced by Johnson and Strom54 in
1989, later modified by Myerson55 in 1997, and refined by Bluman et al56 in 2007. The
Myerson system classifies PCFD into four stages:
Stage I: mild pain and swelling medially, can perform heel rise test with some
weakness, posterior tibial tenosynovitis with no elongation
Stage II: moderate pain and swelling, flexible deformity, weakness with heel rise,
elongated tendon with tears
Stage III: severe pain, fixed deformity, unable perform heel rise, disrupted tendon
Stage IV: ankle tilt in valgus
The 2020 expert consensus considered recently published data and concepts,
particularly the fact that each patient’s clinical presentation varies, with isolated or
combined aspects of the overall deformity not always respecting a linear progression of
events.1
The proposed classification categorizes deformities in two progressive stages: stage I for
flexible deformities and stage II for rigid deformities. Various aspects of the deformities
can occur concomitantly or randomly, depending on individual characteristics and risk
factors, not following a linear progression. Deformities are organized by independent
classes from A to E, allowing stages and classes to be combined and added as findings
are recognized (Table 1).

Figure 21 Images of the foot and ankle of a patient with progressive collapsing foot
deformity who has flexible hindfoot and midfoot deformities. The ankle and the forefoot
are spared. According to the Johnson and Strom classification system, this patient has a
stage II deformity. According to the recent expert consensus classification system, this
patient’s deformity is classified as 1ABD. A, Lateral three-dimensional image shows a
collapsed arch. B, Posterior three-dimensional image shows hindfoot valgus (class A). C,
AP radiograph demonstrates midfoot abduction represented by talonavicular
uncoverage and dissociation between the talar and first metatarsal axis (class B). D,
Lateral radiograph demonstrates arch collapse and no signs of first metatarsal instability
(no class C). E, AP radiograph demonstrates absence of ankle valgus represented by
normal talar tilt (no class E). F, Sagittal CT scan obtained using ticker slices shows no
signs of first metatarsal instability (no class C). G, Coronal CT scan shows absence of
ankle valgus; however, sinus tarsi impingement is observed (class D). (Courtesy of Cesar
de Cesar Netto, MD, PhD, Iowa City, IA.)
Case 2: A rigid hindfoot valgus deformity associated with flexible midfoot abduction,
flexible forefoot varus, and flexible ankle valgus is classified as 1ABCDE (Figure 22).
